Sabina, remember the report I sent to compliance in March? I'm Irfan, the one who kept checking his inbox every hour. Well. Nothing happened. Not a reply, not a 'received'. Six weeks.
At first I thought maybe they were investigating quietly. Then I thought, or maybe it's in someone's drawer. Not knowing was worse than a no.
So I changed what I was doing. I sent a short, polite follow-up: 'I submitted a report on 4 March regarding vendor payments. Could you please confirm it has been received and is being reviewed?' I kept a copy.
Another two weeks. Silence.
Then I spoke to a lawyer, a friend of my uncle's. He explained there's an outside regulator for this kind of thing, and what I'd need to show if I went there. He also said to send one last written request to compliance first, with a date.
I did. And, Sabina, this time they replied in two days: 'Received. Under review.' With a reference number. Sometimes you just have to knock again.

A note to myself, Sunday night. Gurleen.
I'm writing this down because I want to remember how Salma handled it.
At dinner tonight my husband, her Mamu, got loud about the election again. The candidate from our area, the broken roads, 'things aren't safe any more'. Salma is twenty and studies political science, and I could see her getting ready to argue with the slogans.
Instead she put her spoon down and asked him, 'Mamu, what are you actually worried about?' He started the same speech. She asked again, gently. 'For us, I mean. What scares you?'
He went quiet. Then he said the girls come home late from college, the lane is dark, and last year someone's chain was snatched near the temple. 'I just want the house safe.'
Salma said, 'I want that too. We just disagree about who will do it.' The shouting stopped. They talked for another hour, mostly about streetlights.
I have never seen him listen to her like that.

Nazia, you asked how I stopped fighting with my father about politics. I'm Gargi, and it took me two years and one hospital visit to work it out.
We disagreed about everything. The election, the city's new metro line, even which news channel to watch. I used to think my job was to make him see sense. Every dinner was a debate I was trying to win.
Then last year he had a heart scare. Nothing terrible in the end, but I sat by his bed for a night, and I thought: when he's gone, what will I wish I'd done? Not 'won more arguments'. I'd wish I'd laughed with him more.
So I decided. I love him more than I love being right. He isn't going to change his vote, and maybe I won't change mine. That's okay. Now when it comes up, I say what I think, once, calmly, and then I ask about his garden.
We still disagree, Nazia. But we eat dinner together every Sunday now, and it's the best part of my week.

qa.q: How often do Gargi and her father eat dinner together now?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: What was Gargi thinking at her father's bedside?
qa.a: Gargi was frightened of losing him and saw that the arguments would be a regret, wishing for more laughter with him instead.

qa.q: What makes Gargi's new approach work?
qa.a: Saying a view once, calmly, then moving to something they share, so the relationship comes first without Gargi hiding any opinions.

qa.q: How might Gargi's father experience the Sunday dinners now?
qa.a: He probably enjoys them more, feeling close to Gargi even though they still disagree.

grounding: Shows a young person deciding that closeness to a parent matters more than winning political arguments, and accepting that views may not change.

passage:
I'm Charu, Jeevan's younger sibling, and I've watched Jeevan and Amma argue about politics at the dining table for about three years.
It always went the same way. Amma would say something about the government; Jeevan would push back; they would both get louder until one of them left. I started eating in my room in election weeks.
This winter it changed. At dinner Amma said something about the new city tax, and I braced myself. Jeevan said, 'I see it differently, Amma. I think it'll hurt small shops.' Then: 'But you've lived here longer than me.' And Amma said, 'Hmm,' and passed the rasam.
Later I asked Jeevan what had happened. Jeevan said, 'I realised I'm not going to change her mind, and she's not going to change mine. And I'd rather have dinner with Amma than win.'
I can't tell whether Jeevan still gets annoyed inside. But nobody has left the table since December.

qa.q: What did Amma bring up at dinner this winter?
qa.a: The new city tax.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's line 'I'd rather have dinner with Amma than win' reveal?
qa.a: Jeevan values closeness to Amma more than being right, and feels at peace accepting that neither view will change.

qa.q: What else could Jeevan do to keep dinners calm?
qa.a: Keep sharing a view briefly and respectfully, then move on to topics they both enjoy.

qa.q: How do the changed dinners feel for Charu?
qa.a: Charu no longer has to eat alone in election weeks and is relieved that nobody leaves the table any more.

grounding: Shows a young person choosing the relationship with a parent over winning political arguments and accepting lasting differences.
